Scientific Consensus Is Almost Never Wrong Almost

Great article, thanks for posting it. The "muh consensus" argument has to be the most ridiculous and anti-scientific thing to gain popularity in recent years. It makes me cringe even when people use it for things I agree with.

Scientists are not gods, their ponouncements are not scripture. They can and do, both individually and on an institutional level, make mistakes and it's not scientific to take their word as prophesy.

The problem is that laypeople can't handle the scientific principle of "you can't prove a positive". So even when there's overwhelming evidence for something, they'll come back with "but it's not 100% certain, you said so yourself, so it could be wrong." (Just witness the "evolution is just a theory" brigade.) Saying 'it's the consensus of the scientific community' is just a shorter, more acceptable way of saying 'shut up you moron, it's almost certainly true.'

Which is great, except for the little problem that academic consensuses are often formed even when there isn't overwhelming evidence. Heck, sometimes they form even when there isn't an overwhelming consensus.

Totally true. But while sometimes we're wrong about things despite having heaps of good evidence for them (and sometimes we're wrong because we're fallible humans and got too excited even though the evidence doesn't support our conclusion), this doesn't change the fact that unless you're an expert in a given field AND you have solid evidence backing you up, your opinion is vanishingly unlikely to be more reliable than the general consensus.

Nope. If the "experts" are mostly motivated by politics and no one has any significant evidence (because the system they're trying to predict is too complex) then your guess is as good as the consense. Potentially better if it's just blind ideology.

Humans seem to have this insatiable urge to turn everything into a dogmatic belief structure. I think this article helps drive home the point that any scientific position must be falsifiable. Even the most fundamental theories are ready to be dispelled if the right evidence in sufficient quantities is found. I wonder what "consensus" we will laugh about 100 years from now.

Yes, it's one of the more admirable things about the scientific enterprise. I've put it this way in the past, "Science always leaves a door open to doubt and at its best tries to estimate the probability that it is wrong. Science is modest and admits its fallibility and has mechanisms to correct its mistakes. Religion and often philosophy on the other hand claims to be 100% right, and the historical record says that it is 100% wrong whenever matters can be put to a test". Religion's methods of 'correction' leave much to be desired in terms of moral standards.
